abstract_quote: A total of 100 CPR instructional videos were analyzed. While 86% of the videos were produced by healthcare professionals, substantial errors were identified in critical areas such as the extra time spent removing foreign body airway obstruction (67%)
note: Abstract gives n=100 and says videos were 'shared on three major short video platforms in China' but never says they were the keyword-search results screened down from 235 retrieved. The only 'most popular' mention in the abstract refers to a separate sub-analysis of one video per platform, not to how the 100 were chosen.

abstract_quote: The terms "urticaria" and "urtiker" were used as search terms on Google Images. One hundred images were saved for each term
note: Abstract names the search-engine retrieval and the 100-per-term cap but not the words 'first/top'; Methods say 'we evaluated the top 100 search results in both languages'. Conclusion generalises ('urticaria images on Google Images').

abstract_quote: Through a qualitative content analysis of 200 mpox memes shared across major social media platforms, we identified two primary themes
note: Abstract gives n=200 only. Methods reveal hashtag #mpox plus a Google search for 'mpox memes' plus snowballing from comment sections, i.e. a convenience/hand-built corpus.

abstract_quote: 704 web pages were retrieved, of which 320 relevant web pages were included in the content analysis. Among these, 193 web pages (60.3%) published oral health misinformation.
note: Abstract frames the aim as 'the prevalence of oral health misinformation published on web pages in Jordan' and never says the pages came from the TOP Google Trends queries and their top search results.

abstract_quote: This study examines how socio-environmental issues are framed and disseminated in far-right WhatsApp and Telegram groups in Brazil. By collecting and analyzing over 87,962 messages shared from 2023 to 2024
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated. The corpus is a purposively selected population (467 far-right WhatsApp + 136 Telegram groups) and the 34.4% is over ALL links in it, not a top-N cut. The abstract names the far-right group selection; the 34.4% does not appear in the abstract at all.

abstract_quote: we conducted a content analysis of 100 popular TikTok videos. Our findings showed that 55 % of the characteristics that youth attributed to ADHD in their videos did not align with the DSM-5-TR criteria
note: 'popular' names the selection; Methods add that the first 100 videos meeting criteria were taken from a fresh-account #ADHD search. Abstract headline is 55%, whereas the frozen rows carry 52% and 27% - worth checking which figure the rows correspond to.

abstract_quote: Among the 1,000 posts screened, 28 were included. The majority (61%, n = 17) provided non-evidence-based suggestions
note: Abstract gives the 1,000-screened / 28-included funnel but not that the 1,000 were the FIRST 1,000 posts tagged #diastasisrecti, sorted to capture 'the most relevant and popular discussions' (Methods). Also the headline 61% rests on n=28.

abstract_quote: it systematically examined 76,398 comments from 360 of the most relevant videos posted on the day of the event ... Misinformation was pervasive, present in 46% of comments
note: 'most relevant videos' names the relevance-ranked retrieval, though the abstract then generalises to 'Spanish-language public discourse on YouTube'.

abstract_quote: Two research assistants independently coded the top 20 comments and associated replies for each video ... Potential misinformation was present in 10.4 % of comments
note: Abstract names both the top-20 comment truncation and the 15-of-25-video restriction ('Fifteen of these clips had more than 10 relevant comments, for a total of 619 relevant comments'). Clean disclosure.

abstract_quote: content analysis of 200 YouTube news videos ... Sensationalist content attracted higher engagement (30.0%) but had lower credibility, with misinformation prevalent in 38.0% of analysed videos.
note: Abstract gives n=200 with no selection rule. Methods: 'Videos were selected based on recent view counts, sharing [metrics] and topic diversity', i.e. a view-count-ranked, purposively balanced corpus.

abstract_quote: analysing a total of 200 videos published on TikTok in the period prior to the elections in both countries [Spanish original: 'analiza 200 videos publicados en TikTok en el periodo previo a las elecciones presidenciales de ambos paises']
note: Abstract reports no percentages at all; the 2/32/61/5% figures are in the body. Methods state a deliberately purposive build: 'La seleccion se ha hecho en base a que el candidato fuera el protagonista del video y que este tuviera contenido referido a la campana' [the selection was made on the basis that the candidate was the protagonist of the video and that it had campaign-related content], described as 'recoleccion intencionada ... seleccionar de manera estrategica los contenidos que mejor representen el fenomeno' [purposive collection ... strategically selecting the content that best represents the phenomenon].

abstract_quote: Using subreddit data, we analyzed and identified user location based on their interactions within location-specific subreddits ... we examined conversations about COVID-19 and immunization across the U.S., focusing on COVID-19 vaccination.
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated. The corpus is a topic- and geolocation-filtered subset of Reddit comments (5,014 manually labelled), not a top-N cut. The 31.4% never appears in the abstract; the abstract only says regions with lower vaccination rates 'often exhibit a higher prevalence of misinformation-labeled comments'.

abstract_quote: We develop a computational pipeline to identify video accounts with different political leanings that may produce election-related misinformation, collect the videos uploaded by these accounts, and automatically determine which videos are related to ballots
note: Abstract names the account-selection pipeline. The 3.01% denominator is all 5,641 videos from those selected party-aligned/grassroots accounts, so the curation is at account level; no percentage appears in the abstract.

abstract_quote: The top 100 most popular videos from three hashtags (#genderaffirmingcare, #hrt, and #pubertyblockers) were reviewed.
note: Abstract-only record. Selection is named explicitly, but the Conclusion then generalises: 'One in five gender-affirming care videos on TikTok were classified as Misleading' - dropping the top-100/hashtag restriction.

abstract_quote: This chapter investigates the political information ecologies of the "deep vernacular web" by studying the cross-posting of links on 4chan's "politically incorrect" board and a host of political subreddits.
note: Book chapter. The abstract proper names the platforms but not the frequency truncation (only host domains appearing >400 times on 4chan / >2,000 times on Reddit were coded) and gives no n. The 'approximately a third of sources on 4chan and a fifth on Reddit' figure sits in the separate 'Essay summary' section, not the abstract.

abstract_quote: We conducted a cross-sectional content analysis of the 100 most-liked English-language TikTok videos generated by the search term "sunscreen." ... Of the top 100 videos ... 6 (6%) were inaccurate.
note: Clean disclosure: 'most-liked' and 'top 100' appear in both the abstract Methods and the abstract Results.

abstract_quote: We analyzed the top 98 TikTok videos returned for the #adhd hashtag ... Overall, 89% of videos were classified as misleading.
note: Clean disclosure; the conclusion also keeps the qualifier ('highly visible ADHD content on TikTok').

abstract_quote: newly registered accounts were used to search the term "Kawasaki disease" on TikTok and Bilibili, and the top 100 videos from each platform were collected
note: Selection named in the abstract. The 64.58% (31/48 individual-user videos) is not in the abstract, which says only that 'individual-user videos were more often misleading'. FLAG: the frozen row's denominator field is EMPTY for this study.

abstract_quote: Thirty German-language TikTok-videos of each of the six most viewed hashtags on mental disorders ... were classified ... 33.3% (n = 59) as incorrect, 18.1% (n = 32) as overgeneralized
note: Both the 30-per-hashtag cap and the 'six most viewed hashtags' rank criterion are in the abstract. Methods add that the first 30 were taken in the order served by the TikTok algorithm.

abstract_quote: evaluated 240 English-language TikTok videos related to LASIK, LASEK, and SMILE procedures, collected in January 2025 using a newly created account and popular LRS-related hashtags. Videos were included if they had over 1000 views ... 0.4% contained potentially harmful misinformation
note: The abstract names the hashtag frame and the >1000-view engagement floor, but not the fixed per-hashtag quota that produced exactly 240 videos, nor that the search order was used to 'capture the most popular videos on the platform' (Methods).

abstract_quote: Search terms were "COPD", "Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease" and "Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease", and videos with >30,000 views and non-pharmacological content were included ... Among 97 videos, 86% were "useful", 13% "misleading"
note: The abstract names the >30,000-view floor but not that searches were 'sorted by "most viewed"' and capped at the first three result pages (Methods). The conclusion drops the qualifier entirely: 'YouTube videos on non-pharmacological treatment of COPD are of high quality'.

abstract_quote: The search engine Webcrawler was used with the search term "prostate cancer" to generate a list of 75 websites which were reviewed ... Of 943 elements covered on 39 sites, 94% were completely correct, 5% were mostly correct and 1% was mostly incorrect.
note: The abstract names the search-engine retrieval and the 75-site cap but not the word 'top'; Methods: 'The search yielded 390,770 websites, of which the top 75 sites were included in analysis.' The conclusion generalises ('The information on the Internet is of sufficient quality...').

abstract_quote: Online information regarding CFDV was searched using the Google search engine under the Australian domain for four selected search terms and limited to the first 50 results.
note: Explicit first-50 truncation in the abstract. The 24.5% is not in the abstract, which reports a different cut ('consistent with recognized guidelines for almost half of the 157 sites examined'); the frozen row's denominator is the 102 sites that actually stated a timing.

abstract_quote: Using the terms 'contraceptive implant', 'Nexplanon' and 'Implanon', the top 20 results on YouTube by relevance and view count were identified ... A minority (26%) reported misinformation.
note: Top-20-by-relevance-and-view-count stated in the abstract. The 26% denominator is the 23 testimonial videos, a subset the abstract identifies as 'implant testimonial videos'.

abstract_quote: Using the BuzzSumo Application, a range of the top shared health web links in the Polish language social media was assessed ... 40% of the most frequently shared links contained text we classified as fake news.
note: The abstract carries the selection inside the result sentence itself ('40% of the most frequently shared links'), so the percentage cannot be read as a platform-wide rate. Methods: top 10 per keyword, N=80.

abstract_quote: We screened the NewsWhip Insights database for the most shared media articles on Facebook and Twitter ... extracting the 50 most-shared academic articles and media articles covering them ... We accepted the most shared 64 media articles pertaining to 50 academic articles for review ... Fifty-eight percent of media articles were found to have inaccurately reported the question, results, intervention, or population of the academic study.
note: Most-shared selection is stated twice in the abstract, and the abstract even quantifies the coverage ('representing 68% of Facebook and 45% of Twitter shares in 2015').

abstract_quote: We analyzed and quantified 117 user-driven open-ended comments on immunization posted in the Comments section of a Facebook advertisement that targeted Canadian parents ... Inaccurate knowledge (27/130, 20.8%) and misperceptions of risk (23/130, 17.7%) were most prevalent in the 130 nonpositive comments.
note: FLAG: only weakly curated - the corpus is the complete comment set under one Facebook recruitment ad (the ad itself was the most-viewed of two). Also an abstract error: the 130 denominator is CLAIMS coded within 66 negative/hesitant/ambiguous comments, not '130 nonpositive comments'.

abstract_quote: Through a content analysis of stories published by 50 sites that have been labeled fake news and the engagement they generated on social media, we found that stories employed moderate levels of sensationalism, misinformation and partisanship ... Complete fabrications were uncommon
note: Abstract names the pre-labelled fake-news site list but not the cross-match to the 716 most-shared election sites nor the two randomly constructed sampling weeks. No number is given: 'Complete fabrications were uncommon' stands in for the 1.7%.

abstract_quote: The ten most-shared articles on popular social media platforms (Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest, and Reddit) were identified for prostate cancer, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, testis cancer, and PSA testing ... The prevalence of inaccurate or misleading articles was high: prostate cancer (7/10 articles), kidney (3/10 articles)
note: Selection stated; the 30% aggregate appears in the abstract only as per-topic counts out of 10. Methods justify the cut-off explicitly ('articles with lower rankings had a significantly lower' share count).

abstract_quote: we analyzed large volumes of political conversation over a major social media platform - in real-time and native languages during campaign periods - for three major European elections ... we analyze over 4 million tweets from three elections and find that (1) users across Europe shared substantial amounts of junk news in varying qualities and quantities
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated. Denominators are all classified URLs in hashtag-defined election tweet collections, source-coded from a 10% random sample of tweets then applied to the full datasets. The 4.2/10.3/9.1% figures are not in the abstract.

abstract_quote: A systematic search for videos on YouTube addressing treatment options of LUTS/BPH was performed in May 2019 ... A total of 159 videos with median 8'570 views (648 - 2'384'391) were included to the analysis. Only 21 videos (13.2%) were rated to contain no misinformation
note: Abstract says 'a systematic search' and gives n=159 but never that each search term was truncated to 'the 20 videos with the most views' (Methods). Title and conclusion generalise: 'Information on surgical treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia on YouTube is highly biased and misleading'.

abstract_quote: A YouTube search was performed on 21 March 2020 using keywords 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19', and the top 75 viewed videos from each search were analysed ... Nineteen (27.5%) videos contained non-factual information, totalling 62 042 609 views.
note: Top-75-by-views stated in the abstract Methods and repeated in the key-findings box ('More than one-quarter of the most viewed YouTube videos contained misleading information').

abstract_quote: METHODS: Cross-sectional study using a checklist with 14 predefined criteria of 39 websites from 10 countries. RESULTS: All 39 websites mentioned the benefits of antidepressants. Twenty-nine (74%) websites attributed depression to a "chemical imbalance"
note: The abstract Methods give only n=39 and 10 countries. The word 'popular' appears once, in the Objective ('information about antidepressants on popular websites'), which hints at but does not name the procedure: 'we chose easily accessible websites, which appeared at the top of a Google search' (Methods).

abstract_quote: we queried Google for patient-oriented websites and YouTube for consumer videos ... From our PAE-specific searches, we identified 50 websites and 31 videos ... Over a quarter of websites and more than half of videos contained potential misinformation, inaccuracies, or non-evidence-based claims about PAE
note: Abstract names search-engine retrieval but gives no truncation; Methods: the first 20 search results of each of 21 PAE queries (420 results) were screened. Videos additionally required >=100 views.

abstract_quote: We systematically examined responses to questions about the HPV vaccine from the following four most popular smart assistants: Apple Siri, Google Assistant, Amazon Alexa, and Microsoft Cortana. One team member posed 10 questions to each smart assistant and recorded all queries and responses ... A total of 103 responses were obtained from the 10 questions posed
note: The abstract fully describes how the corpus was constructed (10 researcher-written questions x 4 assistants) and flags the 'four most popular' assistants. The 17.5% overall misinformation figure is not in the abstract, which reports accuracy instead and says only that 'Cortana yield[ed] the greatest proportion of misinformation'. The unstated truncation is to first-result-page responses.

abstract_quote: Two search engines (Google and Bing) were used to search for websites offering information about PFP ... After exclusion of duplicates, forty online websites were included in our analyses ... Misleading/inaccurate information was most commonly found in the definition of PFP (20% websites) and clinical examination (15%).
note: The abstract names the search engines but not the first-20-results-per-query cap (80 URLs screened to 40 unique sites). Title asserts the general claim: 'Patients and clinicians managing patellofemoral pain should not rely on general web-based information'.

abstract_quote: A total of 200 of the most viewed YouTube videos from January 1, 2020, to April 30, 2020, were screened, searching in Korean for the terms "Coronavirus," "COVID," "Corona," "Wuhan virus," and "Wuhan pneumonia." ... Of the 105 total videos, 37.14% (39/105) contained misleading information
note: Most-viewed selection stated in the abstract Methods, though the Results sentence itself drops it.

abstract_quote: Com base na coleta dos 100 links mais compartilhados, curtidos e comentados entre maio de 2018 e maio de 2019, por meio da palavra-chave "vacina" [Based on the collection of the 100 most shared, liked and commented links between May 2018 and May 2019, using the keyword "vaccine"] ... as fake news representaram 13,5% dos links com maior engajamento [fake news accounted for 13.5% of the links with the highest engagement]
note: Portuguese abstract. The selection is named twice, including inside the result sentence itself, and the title says it too ('links com maior engajamento' [links with the heaviest engagement]).

abstract_quote: we provide preliminary results from an ongoing investigation on the Twitter diffusion of news pertaining to two classes of sources, namely websites which notably produce disinformation ... opposed to more traditional and mainstream websites which instead publish credible information. We used the Twitter Streaming API to collect a large-scale dataset of thousands of tweets containing links to news articles
note: FLAG: the denominator is set by two hand-built domain lists, so 14.39% is the disinformation share of tweets linking to EITHER list, not a share of all tweets. The abstract names the two-class source design but reports no percentage.

abstract_quote: Using network analysis, this study investigates how information veracity and account verification influence the dissemination of information in the context of discourse about genetically modified organisms on social media.
note: The abstract gives no sample size, no platform (Weibo), no selection rule and no percentage. Methods: 68,237 keyword-matched posts ranked by reposts, top 500 taken, 482 retained.

abstract_quote: In this article, we analysed the 100 most engaging contents about COVID-19 on social networks in Brazil, in March 2020 ... Our results show that misinformation/disinformation accounted for 13.5% of the sample
note: Selection stated, and the result is explicitly framed as a share 'of the sample' rather than of the platform.

abstract_quote: (no abstract - Lancet Digital Health Comment; opening text: "we used big data approaches to analyse Twitter user conversations before and after President Trump's misinformation retweet on July 27")
note: Comment format, no abstract in the archived text. FLAG: not rank-truncated. The 84.4% is over tweets that the biterm topic model clustered onto misinformation-relevant themes and that were then manually annotated (1,237,999 of 2,771,730 collected), so the denominator is a topic-filtered subset, not a top-N cut.

abstract_quote: A Pinterest search was conducted using the term "pelvic organ prolapse," analyzing the first 100 relevant results.
note: First-100 truncation stated. The 27% misinformation figure is not in the abstract, whose Results report only understandability, actionability and quality counts.

abstract_quote: A YouTube search was conducted using the keywords "gout", "gout arthritis", "gout treatment", and "gout diet". Of the 240 videos screened, 114 that met the inclusion criteria were included in the study ... Of the 114 analyzed videos, 87.72% were deemed as useful while 12.28% contained misleading information
note: Abstract gives the funnel (240 screened, 114 included) but not that each search term was cut at 'the top 60 videos' under YouTube's default relevance sort (Methods).

abstract_quote: To evaluate the factual accuracy of shared articles from popular social media platforms ... We used the BuzzSumo search engine to analyze the terms "SB 201", "intersex," "DSD," and "surgery ban" for worldwide social media engagement ... Twenty unique articles with peak activity were analyzed ... 65% of articles were misleading in terms of factual accuracy.
note: Weak but present: 'popular social media platforms' and 'peak activity' signal an engagement ranking, though the abstract never says 'top 10 most shared' per time window as the Methods do. n=20 is small for a 65% headline.

abstract_quote: we curate a dataset of false claims and statements that seek to challenge or refute them. We train a classifier to create a novel dataset of 155,468 COVID-19-related tweets, containing 33,237 false claims and 33,413 refuting arguments.
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated. The abstract describes the classifier-built dataset and gives the raw counts (33,237/155,468 = 21.4%) but never the percentage, and never says the corpus covers only two chosen topics (5G conspiracies and fake cures).

abstract_quote: We analyzed the readability of written transcripts for the first 100 YouTube videos about "Pelvic Organ Prolapse." ... Transcripts with low misinformation (85%) had a higher median readability index (12.6), than transcripts containing high misinformation (12.2).
note: First-100 stated. The 15% high-misinformation figure appears only as its complement ('low misinformation (85%)') and inside a readability comparison rather than as a prevalence statement.

abstract_quote: a careful mapping of psychological profiles of over 2,300 American Twitter users linked to behavioral sharing data and sentiment analyses of more than 500,000 news story headlines
note: FLAG: not a curated corpus. The denominator is all 85,344 national-news links actually tweeted by a linked survey-Twitter panel, i.e. behavioural sharing data; the only curation is the fake-news domain list used to classify them. No percentage in the abstract.

abstract_quote: A total of 615 Facebook comments drawn from Montana news sources were analyzed using the Persuasive Health Message Framework ... A majority (63%) of comments expressed barriers, the most common of which were categorized as either misinformation about the virus or conspiracy theories.
note: Abstract gives n=615 and the source outlets but not the truncation: comments were 'sorted by the number of responses, from the most to least interactive' and only 'the first 100 comments from each news source were taken each day' (Methods). The 34.1% and 19.2% figures are not in the abstract.

abstract_quote: Revisamos sistematicamente los 5 000 tuits mas retuiteados con informacion sobre el zika en ingles [We systematically reviewed the 5,000 most-retweeted English-language tweets about Zika] ... Elaboramos un algoritmo para reconstruir las redes de retuiteo de 266 tuits con informacion erronea y 458 tuits equiparables con informacion veridica [We built an algorithm to reconstruct the retweet networks of 266 misinformation tweets and 458 matched true-information tweets]
note: Spanish translation of an AJPH article. Most-retweeted selection stated in the abstract Methods; the abstract gives counts (266 misinformation tweets) but no prevalence percentage.

abstract_quote: We assessed the reliability, quality, and usefulness of the most-viewed YouTube videos of epidural steroid injection (ESI) ... The top 50 most-viewed videos were assessed ... although 76% were assessed to contain useful information, 8% had misleading information.
note: 'Most-viewed' appears in the Objective, the Methods and the Conclusion of the abstract.

abstract_quote: A YouTube search was performed on April 18, 2021, using the keyword "psoriatic arthritis." ... Of the 200 videos screened, 155 were included in the study after applying the exclusion criteria ... the remaining 23 (14.8%) were misleading.
note: Abstract gives the 200-screened / 155-included funnel but not that the 200 were the first 200 relevance-ranked results, taken because 'most viewers do not go beyond the first few pages of search results' (Methods). The second row (10% of the 10 highest-viewed) is also absent from the abstract.

abstract_quote: We analyze more than 40K audio messages shared in over 364 publicly accessible groups in Brazil, covering six months of great social mobilization in the country. We identify the presence of misinformation in these audios by relying on previously checked facts.
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated. The corpus is every audio message in a set of publicly accessible, politically oriented WhatsApp groups; the curation is at group level (public invite links, political orientation). The 0.6% match rate is not in the abstract.

abstract_quote: We queried YouTube with terms related to donning and doffing of PPE ... Of all videos, 144 were eligible for the analyses. According to misinformation tool, 90 (62.5%) videos contained inaccuracies.
note: 'Of all videos' reads as a census; the abstract never says 'The first 50 videos were examined for each of the 40 keywords combinations. A total of 2,000 videos was achieved' (Methods). Conclusion generalises: 'YouTube may be recommended as a reliable source of information'.

abstract_quote: the top 50 YouTube videos of the non-invasive prenatal testing with the highest number of views were recorded after the exclusion of videos with a non-English language, videos repeated twice and irrelevant videos ... Three (6%) of the videos had misinformation.
note: View-count ranking stated explicitly in the abstract Methods.

abstract_quote: A comparative analysis (including content, thematic and context analyses) of cardiovascular health information published on the websites of AI-funded (n=18, such as 'Drinkaware' and the 'Distilled Spirits Council of the US') and non-AI-funded (n=18, such as 'NHS.uk') organizations based in multiple high-income jurisdictions.
note: The corpus is a hand-picked set of 18 industry-funded and 18 non-industry organisations, and the abstract says so. It reports no percentages at all ('more likely to', 'frequently referenced'), so the 75% and 60% denominators (12 and 10 sources) never surface.

abstract_quote: BuzzSumo, a content research tool, was used to identify the top 10 article links related to transgender fertility most interacted with on the social media platforms of Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest, and Reddit ... The top 10 article links for each time period were examined, with 7,077 total engagements.
note: Top-10-by-engagement stated three times in the abstract. The 25% misleading rate is not reported; the abstract gives an engagement-weighted figure instead ('accurate articles accounted for 74% of the total engagements'). n=20 articles.

abstract_quote: The top 100 most popular videos about ADHD uploaded by TikTok video creators were classified as misleading, useful, or personal experience ... Of the 100 videos meeting inclusion criteria, 52% (n = 52) were classified as misleading
note: Clean disclosure in the abstract Methods; the Conclusion keeps a partial qualifier ('Approximately half of the analyzed TikTok videos about ADHD were misleading').

abstract_quote: We retrieved 167 videos on bladder, prostate, and kidney cancer from TikTok. Only 61 videos (36.53%) met the inclusion criteria and were eventually regarded as sample videos ... 22 posts (36.07%) were misinformative
note: Abstract gives the 167-retrieved / 61-included funnel but not the ranking: 'the results of each keyword we used would be sorted from the most-watched to the least. All relevant videos on the first five pages of the information flow' (Methods).

abstract_quote: We extracted tweets that were published 1 week before and after Musk's disclosure that had received >30 likes and included the terms "Aspergers" or "Aspie" ... We extracted a total of 227 popular tweets ... and 4 (1.8%) as containing misinformation.
note: The >30-likes engagement floor is stated in the abstract Methods and the corpus is called 'popular tweets' in the Objective and Results.

abstract_quote: We also examine whether there are systematic differences in the credibility of sources shared by the subscribers of subreddits that vary by ideology ... conservative subreddits are more likely than liberal subreddits to share articles from sites flagged for publishing COVID-19 misinformation.
note: The abstract describes the ideological subreddit design but never that the credibility figures are computed over only 'the top 20 news sites posted in conservative subreddits' (Results), and gives no n and no percentage. The 25% therefore rests on 5 of 20 sites.

abstract_quote: Search results were sorted by 'views', and the top 150 most-viewed videos were collected and analysed ... Approximately 11% of YouTube's most viewed videos on COVID-19 vaccines, accounting for 18 million views, contradicted information from the WHO or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
note: Exemplary: the qualifier travels inside the headline result sentence ('YouTube's most viewed videos'), in the abstract Methods and in the key-findings box.

abstract_quote: We collected an 8-year time series dataset of public discussion (N = 6,039) on one of the most controversial science issues in China (GMO) from a popular Q&A platform, Zhihu.
note: Abstract gives N=6,039 but not that the corpus is restricted to answers written by the 221 users with more than 10 GMO answers each, i.e. the platform's most active GMO contributors. No percentage in the abstract.

abstract_quote: A search was performed in the video sharing platform YouTube with the keyword "diabetic foot care" on 09.12.2020. From 200 videos, 87 were included in the study ... while 4.6% contained misleading information.
note: Abstract gives the 200/87 funnel but not that the 200 were the search-ranked results the keyword returned (published in the last 8 years).

abstract_quote: In June 2020, we searched Pinterest using "cancer recipe" and "recipe for cancer" at 3 times daily for 2 weeks. Duplicates were removed for a final sample of n = 103 pins ... Health claims were common, with content that purported to prevent (41.8%), treat (27.2%), or cure (10.7%) cancer.
note: The abstract gives the search terms, the sampling schedule and the final n, so the corpus is fully identified as a two-query Pinterest search result rather than Pinterest at large.

abstract_quote: YouTube video results for the search terms "COVID," "coronavirus," and "vitamin D" were collected and analyzed ... In total, 77 videos with a combined 10,225,763 views ... were included in the analysis, with over three-quarters of them containing misleading content about COVID-19 and vitamin D.
note: Abstract gives n=77 but not the truncation: 'search results were collected from the first 3 pages' and 'URLs from the first 60 posts of search results were transferred' at each of two timepoints (Methods).

abstract_quote: A YouTube search was performed using the keyword "vasectomy." The first 100 videos were assessed, with irrelevant and duplicate videos excluded ... False statements regarding vasectomy were made in 14 (17.9%) videos.
note: First-100 truncation stated in the abstract Methods.

abstract_quote: The BuzzSumo analytic tool was used to identify the most frequently shared content about COVID-19 between July and August 2020 ... Among 120 articles that were shared 6,189,187 times in total during the analyzed period ... No myths or misinformation were found in the most frequently shared articles.
note: The selection is stated in the title, the Objective, the Methods and inside the result sentence. A 0% result over the 120 most-shared articles - the framing makes the scope unmissable.

abstract_quote: Our analysis of 200,000 Telegram posts demonstrates that links to known sources of misleading information are shared more often than links to professional news content, but the former stays confined to relatively few channels.
note: The two curated source lists are named, but 'our analysis of 200,000 Telegram posts' reads as a broad corpus when in fact those 202,571 posts are the ones linking to one of the two lists, i.e. only about 3% of all hyperlinked posts. The 37.5% is not in the abstract.

abstract_quote: We developed a search strategy to capture COVID-19 vaccine related tweets, identifying 91,473 tweets between 30 November 2020 and 15 August 2021. The platform's algorithm clustered tweets according to their topic and sentiment, from which we extracted 913 tweets from the top 12 negative sentiment topic clusters.
note: The negative-sentiment cluster truncation is spelled out in the abstract. No percentage is given ('Our analysis also revealed widespread sharing of vaccine misinformation'), so the 9.1% never appears.

abstract_quote: A total of 30,368 campaigns met the criteria for final analysis. After manual review, we identified 53 campaigns (0.17%) seeking funding for alternative medical treatment for COVID-19 ... Moreover, 23 (43%) of the 53 campaigns seeking support for alternative treatments contained COVID-19 misinformation ... Approximately half (71/133, 53%) of these campaigns contained verifiably false or misleading information
note: Best-practice example: every percentage is given with its own denominator, the sub-corpus is expressed as a share of the whole (0.17%, 0.32% of 30,368), and the Conclusion opens with 'A small minority of web-based crowdfunding campaigns'.

abstract_quote: The top posters (ie, tweeters and retweeters) were identified and characterized, along with the most shared Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), most used hashtags, and the 1000 most retweeted posts ... accounting for 22.5% (n=57) of the most shared URLs and 10% (n=107) of the most retweeted tweets.
note: The qualifier travels with each number ('of the most shared URLs', 'of the most retweeted tweets'). FLAG: both frozen rows have an EMPTY denominator field.

abstract_quote: YouTube was searched using the terms "nutrition and COVID-19" in Turkish on 1 February 2021. Videos were filtered according to relevancy, and the first 280 videos were analysed. A total of 218 videos were reviewed ... There were 178 (81.7%) fully relevant and 40 (18.3%) misleading videos.
note: First-280 relevance-ranked truncation stated in the abstract.

abstract_quote: members of the Republican Party in the US Congress have been increasingly sharing links to untrustworthy sources. The proportion of untrustworthy information posted by Republicans versus Democrats is diverging at an accelerating rate ... This study analyses 3.4 million tweets from U.S. American, British and German politicians made between 2016 to 2022.
note: FLAG: not a curated corpus. The denominators are all NewsGuard-rated links posted by a defined set of actors (members of Congress / parliamentarians), so nothing is rank-truncated; the only selection is the actor list, which the abstract names. No percentages in the abstract.

abstract_quote: The 100 most widely viewed videos for the keywords "dental fear", "dental anxiety", and "dental phobia" were chosen for evaluation. Out of the 300 videos, 145 videos met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed.
note: Most-viewed selection stated. The 11.7% is not in the abstract, which only says 'Videos with high views had a higher ratio of misleading information'.

abstract_quote: A total of 374 students were randomly selected from the common first preparatory year college at King Saud University in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and participated by sharing up to three health-related WhatsApp messages per student that they or their relatives had recently read ... Most messages (86%) had either invalid or inaccurate content
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated but participant-elicited. The corpus is whatever messages students chose to hand over ('that they or their relatives had recently read'), which the abstract describes fully; the selection risk is the students' choice of which messages to submit, not a top-N cut.

abstract_quote: Using the key word "varicocele," we retrieved the top 225 videos listed on TikTok in May 2022 ... Thirty-six videos met inclusion criteria ... 23% of videos had misinformation.
note: Top-225 (TikTok's engagement-ordered 'top' sort) stated in the abstract Methods; the 23% denominator is the 36 included videos, which the abstract also gives.

abstract_quote: Medical information related to COVID-19 was analysed in 11 languages ... A total of 562 videos were analysed ... Informative videos (471/562, 83.8%) accounted for the majority, whilst misleading videos (12/562, 2.13%) were minimal.
note: Abstract gives n=562 but not that each language was cut at 'the first 50 relevant results' (75 for English). The Conclusion generalises: 'Misleading videos are often a concern; however, our study found a negligible proportion.'

abstract_quote: We conducted a thorough search on YouTube using 9 search terms related to myositis ... Out of a total of 900 videos, 453 were included for the analysis. Seventy-four per cent and 2% provided useful and not very useful information respectively
note: 'A thorough search' plus the 900/453 funnel, but the abstract never says 'The first 100 videos for each term were' taken in relevance order (Methods). Conclusion generalises: 'A large majority of English YouTube videos on myositis provide useful information'.

abstract_quote: For each procedure, the 100 videos with the greatest views were reviewed ... More than a third (35%) of videos contained misinformation.
note: View-ranked top-100-per-procedure stated in the abstract Methods. The two sub-percentages (45.3% colloquial-term videos vs 20.5% medical-term-only) are reported in the abstract without their denominators, which the paper never gives either.

abstract_quote: we find that among the Tweets that contain a seemingly factual claim while citing a news article as supporting evidence, at least 1% are not actually supported by the cited news and are hence misleading.
note: The filtering chain travels with the number ('among the Tweets that contain a seemingly factual claim while citing a news article'), and the abstract also reports the upstream filter (43.4% not check-worthy). Not stated: the cited article had to come from one of 27 domains drawn from 'the top-50 English-language news sources, as ranked by Alexa Website Ranking' (Methods).

abstract_quote: Videos were identified via targeted keyword searches ... A total of 100 YouTube videos were identified and analyzed ... Of the 100 videos, 70 contained nonfactual information about produce washing.
note: 'Targeted keyword searches' plus n=100, but the abstract never says 'For each search term used, the videos were sorted by view count' with a >1,000-view floor (Methods).

abstract_quote: The top 50 videos populated for the search term 'prostate cancer screening' on YT and TK that met inclusion criteria were retrieved in a cache-cleared browser ... 88% of YT videos and 100% of TK videos had moderate to high levels of misinformation based on screening guidelines.
note: Top-50 stated in the abstract Methods. The 100% TikTok figure rests on 50 videos.

abstract_quote: this study was designed to assess the content, viewer engagement and usefulness of the most viewed YouTube videos on lung cancer ... 167 videos were reviewed, and 143 met the eligibility criteria ... 8 (6%) as misleading
note: 'Most viewed' appears in the abstract Background but not in its Methods paragraph, which gives only the 167/143 funnel; the ranking (sort by views, all videos down to 30,000 views, from 12,500 returned) is in the body. The Conclusion generalises to 'YouTube videos on lung cancer'.

abstract_quote: A total of 100 videos were identified by searching specific keywords in Arabic (Prostate cancer, prostate cancer treatment and prostate) ... Of the 100 retrieved videos, 86% were found to have useful content, while 14% were found to be misleading or irrelevant.
note: Abstract gives n=100 and the keywords but not that the default relevance sort was used to take them. Also a denominator mismatch: the abstract headlines a combined 14% 'misleading or irrelevant', while the frozen row carries 6% misleading.

abstract_quote: Using Application Program Interface, the top 500 TikTok and 120 YouTube videos on overactive bladder were retrieved ... Twenty-three percent of TikTok and 11% of YouTube videos had high misinformation (score >3).
note: Top-500 / top-120 API retrieval stated in the abstract Methods, and the included counts (136 and 75) are given in the Results.

abstract_quote: We test this hypothesis by applying several novel and scalable measures of website monetization strategies to more than 400,000 links shared by 261 anti-vaccine Facebook pages and 190 pro-vaccine ones ... The specific news sites shared by anti-vaccine venues are rated less credible by fact-checking organizations
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated. The denominators are the domain sets shared by two annotated Facebook venue groups; the curation is the venue annotation, which the abstract names. Neither the 50% nor the 0.2% appears in the abstract.

abstract_quote: Finally, we selected the top 100 tweets with the highest number of "likes." ... Of the top 100 cancer-related tweets with the most "likes" that met the eligibility criteria, 44 (44%) contained misinformation
note: The qualifier travels with the headline number, and the abstract also gives the upstream corpus (69,875 extracted tweets). One of the cleanest disclosures in the set.

abstract_quote: We investigated this phenomenon by asking what kind of results users see when they search for information on eleven popular conspiracy theories (CTs) via Google. We analysed links from Google search results (N = 1259) in 12 Western and non-Western countries and 10 languages.
note: The corpus is identified as Google search results with its N, but the abstract does not say the unit is first-page results only. No percentage appears in the abstract; the per-CT figures (5-17% confirming) are in the body.

abstract_quote: Two datasets comprising Italian tweets were analyzed, aiming to uncover primary topics, detect instances of conspiratorial thinking, explore broader emerging topics beyond Silvia Romano's case, and examine whether authors of conspiratorial narratives also engage in spreading misinformation.
note: The abstract gives no sample sizes, no selection rule and no percentage. The 23% denominator is the 653 users who authored tweets in one biterm-topic-model cluster, a selection that exists only in the body.

abstract_quote: This study is based on a content analysis of 238 forwarded messages sent to a public fact-checking group on WhatsApp in Singapore during the first six months of the COVID-19 pandemic ... nearly half of the messages were either partly or entirely inaccurate.
note: Abstract-only record. FLAG: user-submitted, not rank-truncated. The corpus is what people chose to send for fact-checking, so a high inaccuracy rate is close to definitional; the abstract does name the mechanism and frames the aim as 'what types of information people would submit for fact-checking'.

abstract_quote: Descriptive quantitative and qualitative content analysis of 128 reports written by the fact-checkers of Snopes - an established fact-checking organisation - during the period of 24 February 2022 - 28 June, 2023 ... Of the 128 reports, the share of assessments indicative of the invalidity of the claims was 54.7%, while the share of positive ratings was 26.7%.
note: FLAG: fact-checker-selected, not rank-truncated. The denominator is claims Snopes chose to check, so 54.7% describes Snopes's selection rather than the information environment. The abstract names the corpus clearly but its limitations note only warns against generalising to other fact-checking contexts.

abstract_quote: A systematically sampled 10% subset of the data was subjected to qualitative analysis, involving categorisation on content. All tweets assigned to the category of medical resource were assessed for clinical accuracy ... Of 1762 tweets (16%) categorised as a medical resource, 1484 (84%) were medically correct and 240 (14%) were medically incorrect
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated - a systematic 10% sample of all 2019 syphilis tweets. The 14% denominator is the medical-resource subcategory, and the abstract states both the sampling fraction and the subcategory with its n.

abstract_quote: Using the keyword "tumor immunotherapy" in Chinese, we searched TikTok, Tencent, iQIYI, and BiliBili on March 5, 2022. We reviewed the 118 screened videos ... Only 12 videos contained misinformation (score of >1 out of 5).
note: Abstract gives n=118 but not that videos were taken 'in accordance with the video's default "the most viewed" sorting ... and the first 50 videos per website were evaluated' (Methods). The misinformation figure appears as a count, 12 of 118.

abstract_quote: We analyzed the top 40 items that generated the most engagement ... The top 40 items (0.02 % of all items) accounted for 7.71 % of engagements (3,194,900). Four items classified as misinformation accounted for 7.7 % of the Top 40 items
note: Exemplary framing: the abstract gives the top-40 cut, what share of all items it is (0.02%) and what share of engagement it captures (7.71%). Numerical oddity: it reports the misinformation share as '7.7 % of the Top 40 items' although 4 of 40 is 10%, which is the value in the frozen row - the 7.7% looks like the engagement figure repeated by mistake.

abstract_quote: The top 20 videos for each FPF condition were selected based on highest engagement, and 74 videos total met inclusion criteria ... 18% of TikTok videos contained misinformation.
note: Selection stated in the abstract Aims ('the female pelvic floor TikTok videos with the highest engagement') and Methods; the Conclusion keeps the qualifier ('FPF-related TikTok videos with highest engagement').

abstract_quote: HPV-related articles shared on Facebook (2019-2021) were collected using Buzzsumo, a social media analytics tool and analyzed using content analysis ... Of the 138 included articles ... misinformation decreased from 50% in 2019 to 24% in 2021 (p = 0.04).
note: Abstract names the BuzzSumo collection and n=138 but not the engagement ranking behind it: the 50 English-language articles with the highest engagement per year, with an engagement floor of 1,000 (Methods). The 41% pooled figure is not in the abstract; the year-specific rates are.

abstract_quote: A total of 2,700 Internet queries were performed. Across 3 Internet search engines, 25 links of 36 permutations of mRCC keywords and their synonyms were screened for eligibility ... Twelve (31%) websites had >=1 incorrect statement
note: The first-25-links-per-query cap is stated in the abstract Methods, along with the query count and the 39 eligible sites.

abstract_quote: Working on a dataset relative to Italy from December 2019 to August 2020, we validate the choice of the metrics, proving their static and dynamic relations, and their potential in describing the whole system.
note: The abstract gives no sample sizes, no source-selection rule and no percentages; 'a dataset relative to Italy' is all the reader gets. FLAG: all four frozen rows have an EMPTY denominator field, and the corpus is a tracked-outlet source list rather than a rank-truncated sample.

abstract_quote: We collect 13,723,654 posts from 14,532 pages and 11,454 public groups from August through October 2020, posts that together account for nearly all engagement of U.S. public political content on Facebook ... Twenty-three percent of sampled political images (N = 1,000) contained misinformation, as did 20% of sampled images (N = 1,000) containing political figures.
note: The abstract headlines the RANDOM-sample estimates with their N, and the two rank-truncated figures (30% and 26% of the top 300 most-reposted group and page images) stay in the body. A model case of not letting the curated number become the headline.

abstract_quote: Using search terms related to cannabis for pain, the top 66 videos by view count were selected. Each video was classified as useful, misleading, or neither ... Of the 66 videos, 22.73% (n=15) were classified as useful, and 77.27% (n=51) were classified as neither.
note: Top-by-view-count stated in the abstract Methods (top 150 screened to 66 in the body). The 0% misleading is present only by omission: the three categories are named and the counts for two of them sum to 66.

abstract_quote: This is a secondary analysis of the most viewed, contraception-specific TikTok videos that were previously coded as containing educational messaging in a content-analysis study ... The 174 videos with educational content scored as understandable but not actionable
note: 'Most viewed' and 'popular' are both in the abstract. The 12.1% not-evidence-supported figure is not reported; accuracy appears only as a CRAAP subscale mean.

abstract_quote: Videos on each social network retrieved using "hysteroscopy" and "septate uterus" or "uterine septum" as keywords were assessed ... One hundred fifteen videos (47 from YouTube, 35 from TikTok, and 33 from Instagram) were included ... with YouTube exhibiting the lowest rate of inaccuracies compared to TikTok and Instagram. (8.5 % vs. 42.9 % and 36.4 %)
note: Abstract gives the keywords and the per-platform ns but not that 'the first 300 videos reviewed for each social network' were screened under each platform's default algorithm. The 42.9% rests on 35 videos and the 36.4% on 33.

abstract_quote: We performed a summative content analysis on the top 1000 TikTok videos with the hashtag #mentalhealth between October 12 and 16, 2021 ... Advice and information were considered misleading in 33.0% of videos (n = 106)
note: Top-1000-by-views stated in the abstract Methods, and the sub-denominator (319 advice-and-information videos) is given in the same Results paragraph.

abstract_quote: This study examines the circulation of political information and disinformation in 214 public WhatsApp groups during the 2023 electoral campaign for the election of the constitutional council in Chile. Computational and content analysis methods were applied to quantify the proportion of different types of political information that circulated in the groups [Spanish original: 'Este estudio examina la circulacion de informacion politica y desinformacion en 214 grupos publicos de WhatsApp durante la campana electoral de 2023']
note: Spanish/English abstract. It gives the 214 groups but not the viral-message filter behind the denominator: messages repeated more than four times across groups, deduplicated to 342 unique items. No percentage appears in the abstract.

abstract_quote: The top 50 videos on each platform were rated by 4 independent reviewers ... Misinformation was present in 34% of TikTok and 2% of YouTube videos.
note: Top-50 stated in the abstract Methods (YouTube sorted by 'relevance', TikTok by 'top' in the body). The large TikTok-YouTube gap rests on 50 videos per platform.

abstract_quote: This study evaluated TikTok nutrition-related content by (1) identifying common nutrition topics and content creator types; (2) assessing the quality and accuracy of content using evidence-based frameworks ... 55% did not provide evidence-based information, 75% lacked balanced and accurate content ... 18% completely inaccurate.
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated. The abstract gives no sample size and no sampling rule at all, yet headlines six percentages; the body reveals a random sample of 250 posts drawn from 1,054 eligible posts found via nutrition hashtags (#healthyeating, #healthyfood, #diet, #weightloss).

abstract_quote: The analysis draws on a multi-platform, multilingual dataset annotated by professional fact-checkers. Data were collected between March and April 2025 from Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, X/Twitter, and YouTube across four EU Member States ... (iii) data retrieval uncertainty induced by keyword-based data collection.
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated; a keyword-built, fact-checker-annotated sample, and the abstract makes the keyword-selection dependence its central methodological point. No prevalence percentages in the abstract. All four frozen rows have an EMPTY denominator field.

abstract_quote: we analyze the French Twittersphere using ideological inference methods and a matching procedure. Our study is based on a dataset comprising four million tweets and compares 1,907 misinformation sharers with 958 users of similar political orientation who have not shared misinformation (i.e. URL flagged as false by fact-checkers).
note: FLAG: not a curated sample. The 0.05% is the share of all 184M tweets in the full French Twittersphere media-sharing corpus that carry a fact-checked-false URL, i.e. a whole-corpus base rate; it is not reported in the abstract, which is about the matched sharer/control comparison.

abstract_quote: bots emulating "real" users, that collected search results for 48 search queries sorted by 4 search filters for 10 days, yielding a dataset of 915K results. We found that 31.55% of the top-10 search results contained COVID-19 misinformation.
note: The rank truncation is inside the headline sentence ('of the top-10 search results'), and the abstract also states that the queries were curated around 8 COVID-19 misinformation topics, so the topical selection is visible too.

abstract_quote: Twitter shares for the most popular articles were collected at four time periods and misinformation was analyzed for temporal and topical changes ... Twitter articles regarding alternative COVID-19 treatments had the most misinformation (47.5%), followed by transmission (20.0%) and vaccines (8.8%).
note: 'Most popular articles' is stated in the abstract Methods. The pooled 26.3% is not in the abstract; the three topic-level rates are. The closing sentence generalises: 'Overall, there was a high prevalence of misinformation regarding COVID-19 transmission, alternative treatments, and vaccines during the pandemic.'

abstract_quote: The first 50 English-language videos ranked by relevance were evaluated ... Twenty-five videos claimed that chiropractic manipulation could "fix" the Eustachian tube, and 14 videos (28%) asserted nerve correction
note: Abstract-only record. First-50-by-relevance stated. The 50% row appears as a count (25 of 50). The Conclusion generalises: 'Misinformation about chiropractic treatment for OM is widespread and highly viewed on YouTube.'

abstract_quote: Our objective was to analyze the sources, characteristics, tone, and content of the most viewed YouTube videos in Spanish about Covid-19 vaccines ... A total of 118 videos were analyzed ... Hoaxes/conspiracy theories were identified in 1.7% of the videos.
note: 'Most viewed' is in the abstract Objective; the Methods paragraph gives the three search terms and n=118 without repeating the view-count sort.

abstract_quote: In this study we quantitatively assess the phenomenon of misinformation - defined as information which is at variance with widely-accepted scientific consensus - on genetically modified crops and food ("GMOs") in the mainstream and online news media over a two-year period. We found an overall falsehood rate of 9% with a potential readership of 256 million. About a fifth of Africa's media coverage on GMOs contained misinformation
note: FLAG: the abstract headlines two rates with no sample size and no selection rule, and the Africa figure is the worse case - the frozen row records that Africa-region articles were deliberately OVERSAMPLED in the database, which the abstract does not say while asserting 'About a fifth of Africa's media coverage on GMOs contained misinformation'. The corpus is 535 articles from top English-language news media retrieved by Boolean keyword search.

abstract_quote: By semi-automatically matching fact-checked claims with statements from the subtitles of four German news and six talk shows, the study examines the dynamics of these claims. It finds 77 matches in 67 episodes, amounting to 4.85% of the 1382 episodes during the sampling period between June 2023 and June 2024. The rate is higher for talk shows (11.62%) than for news shows (2.28%).
note: FLAG: not rank-truncated - a near-census of all 1,382 episodes of ten named programmes; the only curation is which programmes were picked (the most-viewed German public-broadcast news and talk shows). Every percentage carries its denominator in the abstract.
